posts.title: Corporate Film vs. Brand Film vs. Ad Film: What Your Business Actually Needs
posts.excerpt: Corporate film, brand film and ad film are not interchangeable. Here’s what each one actually does, who watches it, and how to stop paying for the wrong one.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Not sure which format your next video should be? Latch Infinity plans video from the brief backwards - audience first, format second, camera last. Tell us what you’re trying to move and we’ll tell you honestly whether you need a film at all. Sometimes you don’t. We’ll say so.
posts.body:
Every video brief in history begins the same way: “We need a video for the website.”

Three weeks later, deep in pre-production, the truth emerges like a plot twist. The video is also for the trade show booth. And the sales team’s laptops. And the investor meeting. And, someone mentions casually on a Thursday, Instagram.

That’s four films. There is one budget. Nobody is having a good time.

The confusion is fair, to be honest. Corporate film, brand film and ad film all involve a camera, a crew, and a colourist who hasn’t slept. But they answer different questions, they’re watched by wildly different people in wildly different states of attention, and they’re graded against completely different numbers. Picking the wrong one is the most expensive mistake in video - mostly because you only discover it after the money has left the building.

So let’s sort them out.

## The corporate film: proof that you are, in fact, real

A corporate film explains what your organisation does, how it does it, and why it can be trusted to keep doing it on a Tuesday when nobody’s watching. It’s your capability deck, but with a heartbeat.

Its audience is almost always someone already in a conversation with you - a prospect mid- evaluation, a partner doing due diligence, a candidate weighing an offer, an auditor with a clipboard and no sense of humour. Crucially, these people chose to press play. They are not scrolling. That single fact changes everything.

Length: two to five minutes. Contains: facilities, process, scale, certifications, leadership, outcomes. Lives on: the About page, sales decks, tender submissions, reception screens, onboarding. Judged by: completion rate among a small, expensive audience - and whether the sales team actually sends it to anyone.

We worked with a manufacturing client whose plant genuinely wowed anyone who walked through it. Inconveniently, flying a prospect to Bangalore cost more than the margin on a first order. The corporate film existed to shrink that walkthrough into an email attachment. Its success metric was never views. It was how many prospects reached the technical conversation without ever boarding a plane.

The classic corporate film failure? Trying to make it exciting. Slow-motion sparks and an aspirational voiceover do absolutely nothing for a procurement head who has read four hundred capability decks this year. Specificity does. The actual tolerance you hold. The actual test rig. The actual person who runs it, who has opinions about it.

## The brand film: making people feel something long before they need you

A brand film sells a belief, not a capability. Its entire job is to make people who don’t currently need you remember you when they finally do.

Where the corporate film says here’s what we do, the brand film says here’s what we think the world should look like. Usually there’s no product demo. Often no feature list. Sometimes no explicit call to action at all - which makes finance nervous and is, nevertheless, correct. What it has instead is a point of view strong enough to survive being watched once and recalled six months later in a meeting you weren’t in.

Length: 60 seconds to three minutes. Contains: narrative, human characters, a thematic idea, and craft you can feel. Lives on: the website hero, YouTube, LinkedIn, event opens, culture moments. Judged by: recall, shares, the quality of the response - and whether people actually finish it.

Brand films are where cinematography earns its keep. The gap between a competent brand film and a memorable one is almost entirely craft: casting, lighting, sound design, edit rhythm. None of it survives being cheapened. Which leads to an uncomfortable rule: if the budget can’t support proper craft, don’t make a brand film. A mediocre brand film doesn’t communicate “modest budget.” It communicates “mediocre brand.”

The upside is longevity. A good brand film runs for three to five years. Spread across that lifespan, the annual cost is often lower than the ad films you cheerfully bin every quarter.

## The ad film: buying attention, then asking for something

An ad film is built to be interrupted into. It plays before content the viewer actually wanted, inside a feed they were scrolling past, or during a break they used to make tea. It has to win the first three seconds, then convert. No warm-up lap.

Everything about the format follows from that. Hook first, logo later. State the proposition - don’t imply it. Have a call to action, and make it embarrassingly clear. And here’s the part clients resist: ad films work as sets. You test them against each other, and you retire the losers without sentiment.

Length: six to 60 seconds, delivered as multiple cutdowns. Contains: hook, problem, proposition, proof, CTA. Lives on: Meta, YouTube, programmatic, connected TV, cinema. Judged by: cost per view, thumb-stop rate, click-through, and eventually cost per acquisition.

The most useful mental shift for anyone moving into ad film: the deliverable isn’t a film, it’s a campaign asset library. One shoot should produce a whole family - different hooks, different lengths, different ratios, different proof points - because the media buying will tell you within a fortnight which ones deserve money. Making one perfect ad film and running it for a year is how creative fatigue quietly eats your performance while everyone congratulates each other on the edit.

## Choosing: three questions, no jargon

Forget format. Start here.

Who’s watching, and did they choose to? A chosen audience tolerates length and rewards substance - corporate territory. An unchosen audience must be won in three seconds - ad film. An audience you want to influence before they’re in-market - brand film.

What decision are you trying to move? Trust and capability → corporate. Preference and memory → brand. Immediate action → ad.

How long does this need to survive? “Until the next campaign” → build an ad set. “The next three years” → build a brand film and shoot it properly. “Until the product line changes” → corporate film, edited modularly so you can swap sections without a full reshoot.

## The efficient answer: one shoot, three outputs

Here’s the good news. The formats are distinct. The shoot days don’t have to be.

A well-planned two-day shoot at a facility can yield a four-minute corporate film, a 90- second brand film, and six ad cutdowns - provided the shot list was built for all three from the beginning.

That planning is the entire game. Brand film wants performance and controlled light. Corporate film wants coverage and clarity. Ad film wants vertical framing and hook-first composition. Decide all of it on day zero and you get three films for roughly the cost of 1.4. Decide it in the edit and you get one film that does three jobs badly, which is somehow the most expensive outcome of all.

## Where the time and money actually go

One more thing worth knowing before you commission anything, because the cost distribution surprises almost everyone.

Corporate film is cheap to shoot and expensive to organise. The camera work is straightforward. What takes time is access - plant permissions, safety inductions, shutting down a line for twenty minutes, getting a director who is genuinely busy to sit still. Budget your effort in coordination, not in kit. The other silent cost is approvals: corporate films are reviewed by legal, compliance, HR and the MD, often sequentially, often with contradictory notes. Build three review rounds into the timeline and you’ll finish on schedule. Build one and you won’t.

Brand film is expensive to shoot and expensive to prepare. Casting, location recce, art direction, a proper grade and original sound design are where the money goes, and none of them are optional if the film is meant to last three years. The good news is that the approval process is usually shorter, because fewer people feel qualified to give notes on a mood.

Ad film is cheap per asset and expensive in volume. Any single cutdown is trivial. Producing thirty of them, versioned across ratios and lengths, with captions and platform- specific exports, is a genuine post-production project. This is the line item most often underestimated in a scope, and the one that causes the most awkward conversations in week six.

Knowing which curve you’re on lets you brief realistically - and lets you spot a quote that has priced the shoot correctly and the rest of the job not at all.

posts.title: Shooting for Nine Aspect Ratios: How to Plan One Shoot for Every Platform
posts.excerpt: 9:16, 16:9, 1:1 and 4:5: one shoot can feed all of them when framing, safe zones and coverage are planned before production.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity plans every shoot as a multi-ratio delivery from the first storyboard, which is why our vertical cuts never look like they were rescued from a horizontal one at 11pm. Talk to us about your next campaign shoot.
posts.body:
The brief said “one video.”

The delivery folder wants a 16:9 for YouTube. A 9:16 for Reels, Shorts and TikTok. A 4:5 for the Instagram feed. A 1:1 because someone’s legacy placement still needs it. A 2:1 for LinkedIn. Plus 6-second, 15-second and 30-second cutdowns of most of those, in most of those ratios.

That is not one video. That is a spreadsheet wearing a video’s coat.

Handled badly, this matrix is where video budgets go to die - usually in a panicked post- production session where a gorgeously composed landscape frame gets cropped into a vertical one, severing the subject’s head and all of the type. Handled well, it costs almost nothing extra, because every decision that makes it work happens before the shoot, not after.

## Vertical stopped asking permission

The pressure isn’t evenly spread. 9:16 at 1080 × 1920 is now the default for Reels, Shorts and TikTok, and vertical accounts for the overwhelming majority of mobile video consumption. Reported engagement advantages over horizontal on mobile feeds are big - commonly cited around 90% higher - and the reason is embarrassingly simple.

A 9:16 video fills the entire screen. A 16:9 video in a vertical feed occupies about a fifth of it and politely asks the viewer to rotate their phone. Nobody rotates their phone. Nobody has rotated a phone since 2019.

Meanwhile, 16:9 is still absolutely correct for YouTube long-form, websites, and anything destined for a television or a projector. So the answer was never “shoot vertical.” It’s “shoot so both are native, and neither feels like a hostage.”

## The founding principle: shoot wider than you frame

The technique underneath everything else is capturing more resolution than you deliver. Shoot in 4K (3840 × 2160), deliver in 1080p, and you’re sitting on a 2× surplus. That surplus is what lets you pull a full-resolution 1080 × 1920 vertical crop straight out of a horizontal frame - and reposition within the shot in post without the image quietly falling apart.

Two consequences, both of which need agreeing before the shoot, not during it:

Shoot 4K minimum, 6K on hero setups. The extra storage costs less than a sandwich. A reshoot does not. On shots where you know a dramatic vertical crop is coming, 6K or open- gate capture buys you genuine freedom.

Frame for the crop, not the monitor. The operator is composing a 16:9 frame, but the composition that actually matters is the 9:16 rectangle living inside it. This is a real discipline shift, and it’s the single biggest predictor of whether your vertical cut looks intentional or rescued.

## Safe zones: the constraint you can’t see

Every platform cheerfully stacks its own furniture on top of your video. Captions. Usernames. The like-share-comment column. The CTA button. The progress bar.

Put your subject or your text underneath any of it and the viewer gets a beautifully lit elbow behind a “Follow” button. Nobody wins.

For 9:16, the working rule is to keep everything essential - faces, product, on-screen type - in the central band, leaving roughly 250 pixels clear at the top and 400 to 450 clear at the bottom of a 1920-pixel-tall frame. Platforms encroach differently, so build to the greediest one and you’re covered everywhere.

The practical move: load a safe-zone overlay onto the camera monitor. Most modern monitors support custom frame guides. The director and the client watching video village should be looking at the vertical rectangle with the danger bands shaded, not the raw sensor image. One piece of kit, most cropping disasters prevented. Worth the cable.

## Framing habits that survive the crop (and ones that don’t)

Centre your subject vertically. A subject on a horizontal third looks elegant in 16:9 and falls straight off the edge in 9:16. If a shot has to serve both, centre it. Want the third-based composition? Fine - shoot it as a dedicated horizontal-only setup and stop pretending.

Shoot tighter than instinct suggests. Wide establishers are the worst offenders. Crop a wide to 9:16 and you get a sliver of context with a subject the size of a raisin. Plan dedicated vertical establishers instead: a low angle up a building, a corridor receding, anything that’s tall. Verticality is a genuine creative constraint, and vertical-native composition is a different craft - not a lesser one.

Keep negative space above and below. In horizontal, headroom is a cost. In vertical, it’s what keeps your subject clear of the caption band.

Don’t bake horizontal text into the shot. Slates, signs, wall graphics - all of it crops. Add text in post, per ratio, like a person who has learned from experience.

Mind your movement axis. A left-to-right dolly reads beautifully in 16:9 and will happily walk your subject out of a vertical frame mid-shot. Vertical prefers push-ins, tilts, and static frames with movement happening inside them.

## Coverage: the 20% that saves everything

Don’t try to make every shot serve every ratio. That way lies compromise and mild despair. Instead, accept that a handful of shots need dedicated versions.

For every hero moment, capture one horizontal setup and one vertical-native setup. This typically adds 15 to 20% to the shooting schedule - not 100% - because the lights, the talent, the location and the crew are already standing right there, drinking chai.

Put the supplement in the schedule explicitly. The failure mode is calling it “we’ll grab it if there’s time.” There is never time. There has never once been time.

## Post: build one master, derive the rest

Structure the edit so ratios are derivatives, not separate projects with separate opinions.

Cut the 16:9 master first - it’s usually the longest and most complete version, and it enforces narrative discipline. Then duplicate the sequence and reframe shot by shot for vertical. Auto-reframe tools have genuinely improved and make a decent first pass, but they track motion, not meaning. In a two-shot, they will follow the wrong face with total confidence, every single time.

Rebuild graphics per ratio. Never scale them. A lower third designed for 16:9 becomes an eye test in 9:16. Design a small system with a horizontal and a vertical variant of each element and the rebuild takes minutes instead of afternoons.

Export everything from one colour-graded master. Nothing torpedoes a campaign faster than the vertical cut arriving half a stop darker than the horizontal one, and nobody noticing until the client does.

## The deliverables checklist

Agree this at the brief stage. Not the delivery stage. The brief stage.

- 16:9 (1920 × 1080) - YouTube, website, events
- 9:16 (1080 × 1920) - Reels, Shorts, TikTok, Stories
- 4:5 (1080 × 1350) - Instagram and Facebook feed
- 1:1 (1080 × 1080) - legacy feed placements
- Cutdowns: 6s, 15s, 30s and full length, per ratio as required
- Captioned and uncaptioned versions of each
- A subtitle file (.srt) per language

Write it into the scope. Every ratio that appears after the shoot costs roughly ten times what it would have cost before it, and about forty times the goodwill.

## The tenth ratio nobody counts: sound off

There’s one more format constraint hiding inside all the others, and it doesn’t appear in any specification sheet.

A very large share of feed video is watched with the sound muted - on a commute, in an office, in bed at 1am next to a sleeping person. Which means your beautifully mixed voiceover is, for a substantial portion of the audience, not happening at all.

The implications are structural, not cosmetic:

Captions are content, not accessibility compliance. Burn them in for social cuts rather than relying on platform auto-captions, which are inconsistent, unbranded and frequently wrong about proper nouns. Style them as part of the design system - position, weight, colour, the way they animate.

The first three seconds must work silently. If your hook is a spoken line, half your audience never receives it. Put the hook on screen as well, or build it visually.

Design for the caption band. This is the practical link back to safe zones - captions occupy real estate at the bottom of the frame, which is precisely where inexperienced editors like to put lower thirds.

Then mix properly anyway. The audience that does turn sound on is your most engaged segment, and they notice when the audio is thin. Sound-off design is an addition, not a replacement.

Treat “sound off” as an eleventh deliverable in the matrix and you’ll stop losing the half of the audience that never heard a word.

posts.title: Campus Films That Actually Drive Admissions: What Universities Get Wrong
posts.excerpt: Most university campus videos are the same. Here’s what prospective students actually watch and how to build a campus film that moves applications.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity builds learning and brand content for universities across India, and we plan campus films around the admissions funnel rather than the campus map. Talk to us about your next admissions cycle, or see how our EdTech practice supports institutions end to end.
posts.body:
Watch ten Indian university campus films back to back and a strange thing happens. You start predicting them.

Drone rises over lawn. Students walk purposefully in slow motion, laughing at a joke nobody told. Library. Lab, someone holding a pipette with great significance. Cricket match. Vice-Chancellor addresses camera on the subject of holistic development. Strings swell. Logo.

It’s competent. It’s also structurally identical to the film made by the institution ranked twenty places above you and twenty places below you. And it is doing approximately nothing for admissions, because it’s a confident answer to a question nobody asked.

## What prospective students are actually up to

The behaviour is well documented and slightly humbling. Around 78% of prospective students start their research on Google. Video is overwhelmingly the format they want - roughly 72% say they prefer virtual tours and video over traditional brochures. Nearly 90% of teenagers use YouTube, about three-quarters of them daily.

But here’s the finding that should reshape your entire content plan: day-in-the-life vlogs pull roughly three times the engagement of promotional campus videos.

Students aren’t searching for institutional positioning. They’re searching for a simulation of their own life on your campus. The institution makes a film about the institution. The student wants a film about themselves. That gap is where the money disappears.

## Mistake one: opening on the drone

The aerial exists for two reasons - it’s the most expensive-looking image available per rupee, and campus decision-makers are genuinely proud of the campus. Both are true. Neither is a viewer benefit.

A 17-year-old scrolling YouTube has no idea what your buildings look like from 120 metres and no frame of reference to be impressed by it. Worse, the aerial opening is the single most generic three seconds in higher education marketing - spent at the exact moment the viewer decides whether to stay.

Open on a face. A hand. A specific human doing a specific thing. If you must use the aerial, drop it in the middle as a transition, where its geographic information is actually doing a job.

## Mistake two: casting for polish instead of candour

The students in most campus films were chosen by the marketing team for being articulate, presentable and - the real criterion - available on shoot day. They deliver flawless lines about world-class faculty and excellent placement opportunities.

Viewers detect this instantly. It reads as advertising, and advertising is what they were trying to see past.

The students who actually convert sound like they’re talking to a friend, not a lens. They mention the specific thing they were nervous about before joining and what actually happened. The fix is unglamorous: interview twenty students with no script, ask what surprised them, and build the film out of the answers. Cast for candour. The best line in a campus film is almost never in the brief - it’s the thing someone says while the crew is packing up.

## Mistake three: one film, four audiences, zero fit

An engineering aspirant, a design aspirant, an international applicant and a parent want four completely different things. One institutional film tries to serve all of them and quietly serves none.

Parents want safety, structure, placement outcomes and cost. Domestic aspirants want peer culture, hostel life and what the campus is like at 10pm on a Wednesday. International students want visa support, food, community and airport logistics. Programme aspirants want the labs, the studios, the faculty in their discipline.

Modular beats longer, every time. From one production block, build:

- A three-minute institutional film for the homepage and formal contexts
- Six to eight programme-specific films at 90 seconds each
- A day-in-the-life series, largely shot by students themselves
- A parent-directed film on safety, outcomes and support
- A pile of vertical cutdowns for Instagram and YouTube Shorts

One crew, one week, one grade. Four audiences, each getting a film that was actually made for them.

## Mistake four: shooting when the campus is asleep

Campus films are usually shot in whichever week the crew was free - which is often a quiet week, because that’s when timetables permit. The result is empty corridors, a canteen with three people in it, and a campus that reads as recently evacuated.

Shoot during peak chaos. Fest week. Open day. Exam season. First week of term. A full, noisy, alive campus communicates belonging in a way no voiceover has ever managed. If the calendar forces a quiet week, plan and cast your crowd scenes deliberately rather than hoping some students wander through.

## Mistake five: no vertical, no Shorts, no plan

A four-minute 16:9 film uploaded to the website and a YouTube channel with 900 subscribers is not a distribution strategy. It’s a filing system.

Prospective students are not visiting your channel. They’re being served things in a feed. So every campus production should also generate a library of vertical short-form assets built for discovery: a hostel room tour, a canteen taste test, the walk from the main gate to the department, three students on “what I wish I’d known before joining.” These cost very little alongside the main shoot and they’re the only assets that reach people who’ve never heard of you.

Then pair them with the formats that convert further down: virtual tours, which convert a meaningful share of attendees into inquiries when run as live events, and personalised video messages from admissions, which have been linked to notable lifts in commitment rates.

## What a good campus film does instead

It answers a question. “What’s it actually like to study here?” is a far better brief than “showcase our campus.”

It’s specific. The professor who runs the robotics lab. The dish everyone queues for. The 24-hour reading room. The exact bus that goes into the city. Specificity is what makes a place feel real and a film feel true.

It shows the ordinary. Not just convocation and fest. The walk to class in the rain. The empty studio at midnight. The group project argument. Prospective students are trying to picture a daily life, not a highlight reel.

It has a next step. Every film should land somewhere concrete - the programme page, the application, a campus visit booking, the WhatsApp counsellor. A film that ends on a logo has thrown its conversion in the bin and walked away.

## Measuring it like you mean it

Views are not the metric. Views have never been the metric.

Track completion rate by audience segment, click-through from video to programme page, assisted conversions where a video view precedes an application, and enquiry attribution asking new applicants where they first encountered you.

If a film can’t be tied to a measurable step in the admissions funnel, it’s a brand asset rather than an admissions asset. That’s a perfectly respectable thing to be - it just needs to be budgeted and judged as one, rather than defended at the end of the year as though it were both.

## The cheapest content you’re not making

Here’s the awkward economics of campus video: the content that performs best is often the content that costs least.

Student-generated content - a hostel tour shot on a phone, a genuine reaction to results day, a room makeover, an exam-week vlog - routinely outperforms professionally produced films on the platforms where discovery actually happens. It’s not because production quality doesn’t matter. It’s because credibility matters more, and a polished film is inherently less credible as testimony than a shaky one.

The mistake institutions make is either ignoring this entirely or over-managing it into oblivion. A student ambassador programme with a 12-point brand guideline and a three- stage approval process produces content that looks exactly like marketing, which defeats the entire purpose.

A workable middle path:

- Recruit 8 to 12 student creators per intake, across programmes and backgrounds, and pay them properly. Free pizza is not a content strategy.
- Give them prompts, not scripts. “Show us your Sunday” produces better results than “highlight our library facilities.”
- Set three non-negotiables, not thirty: no other students filmed without consent, nothing filmed in restricted areas, nothing that misrepresents facts about the programme.
- Review for those three things only. Resist the urge to note that the room was untidy. The untidy room is the point.
- Give them equipment and editing support, not creative direction. A decent mic and a tripod raise the floor without flattening the voice.

Run alongside your professional production, this gives you two content streams with different jobs: the crafted films that carry the institution’s positioning, and the honest ones that answer the question every applicant is actually asking - what would my life be like here?

posts.title: From SLM to Screen: Turning a Word Document into a Lecture Students Finish
posts.excerpt: A 40-page Self Learning Material file is not a lecture script. This production process turns compliant course documents into videos students finish.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity builds end-to-end 4-Quadrant learning solutions - academic content, e- learning assets, compliance-led quality assurance and LMS-ready deployment, all under one roof. Explore our EdTech practice or send us a unit and we’ll show you what it looks like on screen.
posts.body:
Somewhere on a university server right now sits a Self Learning Material document. Forty pages. Times New Roman. A table of contents, five units, learning outcomes at the top, MCQs at the bottom, references formatted with real care.

It is academically sound. It has passed review. And someone has just been asked to “turn it into videos by the end of the month.”

This is where most e-learning production goes sideways - not because the source material is bad, but because a document and a lecture are fundamentally different animals wearing similar clothing. A document is scanned. A lecture is endured. Readers skip, re-read and control their own pace. Viewers get one pass, in one order, at a speed someone else chose.

Reading a document aloud over slides is not a lecture. It’s a hostage video with better typography.

Here’s the process that actually works.

## Step one: audit the document as content, not as a script

Before a single slide is designed, read the SLM with one question running: what is the actual teaching here?

Most units contain three types of material, and they need three completely different treatments.

Conceptual content - definitions, frameworks, models, cause-and-effect. This is what video is genuinely brilliant at, because it can animate a process the page can only describe.

Procedural content - steps, calculations, methods. Video handles this well when demonstrated, badly when read.

Reference content - tables, extended lists, statutory provisions, bibliographies. Video is the worst possible medium for these. They belong in a downloadable, not on screen at 1080p where nobody can pause fast enough.

Sort the document into these three buckets first. Typically 50 to 60% of an SLM survives into video, 20% becomes an on-screen job aid, and the rest stays happily as a document. Trying to film 100% of it is the original sin of e-learning production.

## Step two: restructure around attention, not around headings

The document’s chapter structure was built for a reader with a table of contents and a highlighter. Video needs a structure built for someone whose attention is under active attack from a phone in the same hand.

The unit of video is not the chapter. It’s the segment - six to ten minutes covering one idea, with a clear opening question and a clear resolution. A 40-page unit typically becomes five to eight segments, not one 55-minute recording.

This isn’t only about attention spans. Segmented content is searchable, re-watchable, and re-usable across programmes. When a syllabus changes, you re-record one eight-minute segment rather than an entire lecture.

Within each segment, restructure from heading order to question order. Academic documents typically move definition → explanation → example → application. Video works far better in reverse: a concrete situation, the problem it poses, then the concept that resolves it, then the formal definition. Same content, same rigour - just sequenced so the learner has a reason to want the definition by the time it arrives.

## Step three: write a script, not a narration

The most common failure in the entire pipeline is handing a voice artist the document and pressing record.

Written academic prose has long sentences, subordinate clauses, passive constructions and nominalisations (“the implementation of the framework requires the consideration of…”). All of it is perfectly readable and completely unlistenable. The ear can’t hold a 40-word sentence with three dependent clauses. It gives up around word 25 and starts thinking about lunch.

Spoken script rules that make a measurable difference:

- Sentences under 20 words. Most under 15.
- Active voice, almost always.
- One idea per sentence.
- Signposting the page doesn’t need: “There are three of these. Here’s the first.”
- Contractions. People say “it’s.” Formality lives in your rigour, not your syllables.
- Read every line aloud before it’s approved. If you run out of breath, so will the presenter.

Critically, the script must preserve the academic substance exactly. Simplifying the language is required. Simplifying the content is a compliance problem, and in a regulated programme it’s the kind that surfaces during an audit.

## Step four: design visuals that carry meaning, not decoration

Slides in most recorded lectures are the script, in bullet form, in a smaller font. This is the worst configuration available, because it forces learners to read and listen simultaneously - two channels competing for the same processing capacity. Learning outcomes suffer measurably.

The alternative: the visual carries what words can’t.

- Processes become animated flows that build step by step as the narration reaches them
- Comparisons become side-by-side structures, not bulleted paragraphs
- Data becomes a chart with one highlighted takeaway
- Abstractions become a concrete metaphor, drawn
- Definitions get four words on screen, not the full sentence being spoken

A useful discipline: if a slide would still make sense with the audio muted, it’s probably a document page in disguise. Slides should be incomplete without the narration, and the narration incomplete without the slides.

## Step five: production choices that survive scale

Most institutions need dozens of hours, not one showpiece. Production design should optimise for repeatability.

Presenter on camera or voice-only? On-camera presence improves engagement and trust, particularly in the opening and closing of each segment. A workable hybrid: presenter on camera for the first 45 seconds and the last 30, voice-over graphics in between. You get the human connection without needing a faculty member to be film-ready for eight straight hours.

One consistent set. A single lighting and camera setup, locked and documented, means episode 40 matches episode 1. Photograph the setup. Write down the settings. Future you will be extremely grateful.

Teleprompter, without the stare. Faculty reading from a prompter often develop the distinctive glassy gaze of a hostage. Position it just under the lens, rehearse once, and let them paraphrase. Slight imperfection reads as authority. Perfect delivery reads as a recording.

Record audio properly. Viewers forgive mediocre picture and abandon bad sound within seconds. A lavalier and a treated room outperform an expensive camera in a reverberant hall, every time.

## Step six: build for the LMS from day one

“LMS-ready” is not a file format - it’s a workflow. Decide before production: the video platform and its encoding requirements, the SCORM or xAPI packaging standard, caption and transcript requirements for accessibility, chapter markers, the assessment items that sit alongside each segment, and the file naming convention that maps every asset back to its unit and outcome.

Decide this after production and you’ll spend as long repackaging as you spent shooting. Ask anyone who has renamed 340 files by hand.

## Step seven: quality-check against the source

The final pass is the one people skip. Put the original SLM next to the finished video set and verify: is every learning outcome addressed? Is every mandated topic covered? Are definitions verbatim where regulation requires it? Do the assessment items still map to what was taught?

The video is a derivative of a compliance-approved document. If it drifts, the compliance approval doesn’t travel with it - and in a regulated programme, that’s not a content problem. That’s an audit finding with your name on it.

## Accessibility and language: decide early or pay twice

Two requirements get treated as post-production extras and are, in practice, structural decisions that need making before the first script is written.

Accessibility. Captions and transcripts are mandatory in most regulated programmes and non-negotiable in good practice. But real accessibility goes further than a subtitle file. Any information conveyed purely visually - a chart, a diagram, a colour-coded distinction - must also exist in the narration or a text alternative, or a learner using a screen reader receives an incomplete unit. This is a scripting decision. If the voiceover says “as you can see here,” the visual has just become load-bearing and inaccessible in the same breath. Write narration that stands alone, and the accessibility work largely takes care of itself.

Language. If the programme will be delivered in more than one language, the entire production changes shape. On-screen text must live in editable graphics layers rather than baked into the video. Narration should be recorded to a locked picture so alternate voice tracks can be swapped without re-editing. Idioms and culturally specific examples need flagging at script stage, because they don’t translate - they need replacing, and that’s an academic decision, not a translator’s.

Retrofitting either of these into a finished library is roughly as expensive as producing it again. Deciding both at the brief stage costs a conversation.

posts.title: Gamification in Corporate Training — Beyond Points and Badges
posts.excerpt: Points, badges and leaderboards are the least interesting part of gamification. Here’s what actually drives engagement and retention in corporate learning.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity turns live events into real-time multiplayer experiences and builds gamified learning that goes well past points and badges. See how our gamified experiences work, or tell us about your training problem.
posts.body:
There’s a particular kind of corporate training module that has been “gamified.” You complete a chapter, a badge appears. It is bronze. Later, it becomes silver. There is a leaderboard on which you are 47th out of 312, and you have never once wondered who is 46th.

Nobody is playing anything. A progress bar has been painted onto a compliance module and everyone has agreed to call it a game.

The frustrating part is that the underlying idea is thoroughly evidence-backed. Gamification is associated with roughly a 48% lift in engagement. Retention of material improves by around 40%. Some 90% of employees report feeling more productive in gamified environments, and organisations using gamification report noticeably better employee retention - with figures like 69% of employees staying three or more years appearing in industry surveys.

Those numbers don’t come from badges. They come from mechanics that badges are a lazy proxy for. So let’s talk about the actual mechanics.

## What games are really doing

Strip away the theme and every good game runs the same engine: a clear goal, meaningful choices, immediate feedback, escalating difficulty matched to growing skill, and a tolerable cost of failure.

Notice that points appear nowhere in that list. Points are a scoreboard for the engine. Bolting a scoreboard onto a system with no engine produces exactly what most corporate gamification produces - a number that goes up while nothing interesting happens.

Look at any training module through that engine and the diagnosis is usually immediate. Is there a goal beyond “finish this”? Are there real choices, or just a next button? Is feedback immediate, or does it arrive as a score at the end? Does difficulty escalate? Is failure survivable and informative, or terminal and punitive?

Most compliance modules score zero out of five. Then a badge is added, and they score zero out of five with a badge.

## Mechanic one: decisions with consequences

The most powerful thing you can put in corporate training isn’t a reward. It’s a decision that could go wrong.

Instead of explaining the escalation policy and then quizzing on it, drop the learner into a scenario: a customer is angry, the policy is ambiguous, three options are available, and each one leads somewhere different. Two are defensible. One creates a problem that surfaces three screens later.

This is branching scenario design, and it works because it recruits genuine cognitive engagement. The learner isn’t recalling a rule - they’re applying judgement, which is the actual skill the training exists to build. It also produces something a quiz never will: the memory of having got it wrong, which is remarkably durable.

Repetition, decision-making and instant feedback are consistently identified as the mechanisms behind gamification’s retention advantage. Branching scenarios deliver all three at once.

## Mechanic two: feedback in seconds, not at the end

Games tell you instantly. Miss a jump, fall. No end-of-module report, no email on Thursday.

Corporate training routinely delays feedback by minutes or days, which severs the link between action and consequence - the exact link that learning depends on. Feedback that arrives after the learner has moved on is information, not learning.

Practical fixes are unglamorous and effective: response-level feedback rather than end-of- quiz scores; explanations of why an answer was wrong, not just that it was; visible consequence within the scenario itself; and progress indicators tied to demonstrated capability rather than screens viewed.

## Mechanic three: difficulty that actually escalates

Most training is flat. Question 1 and question 20 are equally hard, which means the module is either boring for the capable or punishing for the new - and usually manages both across different people.

Adaptive difficulty fixes this: learners who demonstrate mastery skip ahead, learners who struggle get additional scaffolding. It’s more work to build, and it’s the difference between a module people tolerate and one they finish.

Even without adaptive technology, deliberate escalation helps enormously. Structure content so early scenarios are clean and later ones are genuinely ambiguous - the messy, real cases where two policies conflict and the right answer requires judgement. That’s where the learning lives anyway.

## Mechanic four: social, but not a leaderboard

Leaderboards are the most-deployed and least-effective social mechanic in corporate learning. They motivate the top 10%, demoralise the bottom 50%, and are quietly ignored by everyone else. Worse, in a workplace they can encourage exactly the wrong behaviour - completing fast rather than learning well.

Social mechanics that work better:

Team goals. Shared progress toward a collective target creates positive peer pressure rather than ranking anxiety.

Peer visibility of contribution, not rank. “Fourteen people in your team have shared a tip this week” beats “you are 47th.”

Collaborative problem-solving. Scenarios that require two people with different roles to solve together - genuinely engaging, and they teach the cross-functional communication most organisations are quietly missing.

Real-time multiplayer at live events. This is where gamification gets genuinely fun. Turning a town hall or sales conference into a synchronised multiplayer experience - attendees joining from their phones, competing and collaborating live - produces engagement levels that no slide deck has ever approached, and generates real data about what your teams know.

## Mechanic five: rewards that mean something

If you’re going to use rewards, make them matter.

Extrinsic rewards work when they’re scarce, meaningful and visible to the right people. A badge that everyone earns for finishing is none of the three. Recognition from a senior leader, a genuine skill certification, early access to something desirable, a real budget for a chosen project - these carry weight.

But the strongest rewards in learning are usually intrinsic: competence, autonomy and relatedness. A module that leaves someone feeling more capable at their job tomorrow has delivered a better reward than any badge, and doesn’t require an administrative system to sustain it.

## What not to gamify

Worth saying plainly, because enthusiasm for this stuff tends to overshoot: some training should not be gamified, and forcing it produces something worse than a plain module.

Anything where speed is the wrong incentive. Safety procedures, clinical protocols, financial controls. Introduce a timer or a leaderboard and you have explicitly rewarded haste in exactly the domain where haste kills. If you gamify these at all, reward accuracy and thoroughness, and make speed irrelevant.

Sensitive human topics. Harassment prevention, mental health awareness, grievance procedures, bereavement policy. A points system attached to a module about workplace harassment communicates that the organisation regards it as trivia. People notice. It undermines the entire message.

Anything mandatory and legally defensible. Where the training exists partly to demonstrate that everyone completed it, elaborate mechanics add cost and risk without adding defensibility. Make it short, clear, well-designed and honest about what it is. A five- minute module that respects people’s time earns more goodwill than a twenty-minute one dressed as a quest.

Content that changes monthly. Game design is expensive to build and expensive to update. Reserve it for stable, high-value competencies that will be taught for years - not for the product update deck.

The rule of thumb: gamify judgement, not compliance. Where the learning objective is “know this,” write it clearly and get out of the way. Where the objective is “decide well under ambiguity,” that’s where the mechanics earn their cost - and where they’re genuinely, measurably better than anything else available.

## What to do on Monday

Take your worst-performing training module. Don’t add points. Instead:

1. Find the three decisions the role actually requires, and build a branching scenario for each.

2. Move all feedback to the moment of action. 3. Make the last third genuinely harder than the first. 4. Replace the leaderboard with a team goal. 5. Cut the module in half - most are twice as long as their content justifies.

Measure completion rate, assessment scores at 30 days rather than immediately, and - the metric that matters most and gets measured least - observed behaviour change on the job.

If those move, you’ve built a game. If only the badge count moved, you’ve built a scoreboard with nothing behind it.

posts.title: A Logo Is Not a Brand: What Goes Inside a Real Brand Book
posts.excerpt: A logo file is not a brand identity. Here’s what a proper brand book contains, why it matters and how to tell one from a glorified logo sheet.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity builds brand books that designers can actually work from - strategy, system, voice and governance, not just a logo in three colourways. Explore our branding practice or send us your current guidelines and we’ll tell you what’s missing.
posts.body:
There is a specific PDF that has been emailed to every designer, printer, agency and intern in your organisation. It’s eight pages. It contains the logo, the logo in white, the logo in black, a rule about minimum clear space, two hex codes, and a page nobly titled “Incorrect Usage” featuring the logo stretched and rotated as a warning to others.

It is called the Brand Guidelines. It is a logo sheet in a nice suit.

You can tell it’s a logo sheet because of what happens next. Someone needs to design a recruitment ad, and the document has nothing to say. Someone writes a product email and invents a tone of voice on the spot. Someone builds a landing page and picks a button colour that appears nowhere in the palette because the palette has two colours and neither works as a button. Within eighteen months the brand looks like six brands in a trench coat.

A real brand book prevents this. Here’s what’s in one.

### 1. The strategy the identity is built on

Every visual decision should be traceable to something non-visual. Without this section, the brand book is a set of aesthetic preferences that any confident person can override in a meeting.

At minimum:

- Purpose - why the organisation exists beyond revenue
- Positioning - the specific space you occupy relative to competitors, in one uncomfortable sentence
- Audience - who you’re for, and, more usefully, who you’re not for
- Personality - three to five traits, each with an explicit opposite pole (“confident, but not arrogant”)
- Promise - what the customer can reliably expect every time

This section is short - usually four to six pages - and it’s the part that settles arguments. When someone asks “should we do a Diwali post?”, the answer comes from here, not from taste.

### 2. The logo system (not the logo)

A brand does not have a logo. It has a logo system: a primary lockup, a horizontal variant, a stacked variant, a symbol-only mark for small applications, and a favicon that survives being 16 pixels wide.

For each, the book specifies minimum size, clear space, approved colour treatments, and - crucially - which context uses which. “Use the stacked lockup when the available width is under 200px” is a useful instruction. “Don’t distort the logo” is not; nobody has ever distorted a logo on purpose.

Also here: co-branding rules. How your mark sits beside a partner’s, a client’s, a certification body’s. This page gets used far more than anyone expects and is missing from almost every brand book we’re shown.

### 3. A colour system that survives contact with reality

Two hex codes is not a colour system. A working palette has:

- Primary colours with values for every space - HEX, RGB, CMYK, Pantone, and RAL if you produce anything physical
- Secondary and accent colours with defined proportions (“primary 60%, secondary 30%, accent 10%”)
- Functional colours - success, warning, error, information - because your product interface needs them and will otherwise invent them
- Neutrals - a proper greyscale ramp, typically five to seven steps
- Accessibility pairings - which text colours pass WCAG AA on which backgrounds, stated explicitly

That last one is where most brand books collapse. A gorgeous light-grey-on-white combination that fails contrast standards will either be used and exclude people, or quietly abandoned in favour of something off-brand. Test the pairings and publish the results.

### 4. Typography with actual hierarchy

Naming two typefaces isn’t typography. The book needs a type scale - display, H1 through H4, body, caption, legal - with sizes, weights, line heights and letter spacing for each, specified for both print and screen.

It also needs licensing information (who owns the licence, how many seats, what the web font licence permits) and a documented fallback stack for when the licensed font isn’t available - in an email client, in a Word template, on a partner’s system. Without a sanctioned fallback, people pick their own. Usually Calibri. Sometimes worse.

### 5. Photography and image direction

The single most-ignored section, and the one that does the most damage when it’s missing. Two organisations with identical logos and palettes can look entirely different based on imagery alone.

Specify subject matter and situations, composition style, colour treatment and grade, lighting approach, the treatment of people (candid or posed, looking at camera or away), what’s explicitly off-limits - and, most valuably, a mood board of ten approved reference images alongside ten rejected ones with reasons. Designers learn more from the rejections than from the rules.

### 6. Iconography, graphics and the supporting kit

The visual elements that appear everywhere and get invented separately in every department: icon style (line weight, corner radius, grid), illustration approach, patterns and textures, data visualisation styling, and the shape language that makes a layout recognisably yours even with the logo removed.

That last test is a genuinely good one. Cover the logo. Is it still obviously you? If not, the identity is doing less work than you think.

### 7. Voice and tone

Half of what your brand puts into the world is words, and most brand books ignore them entirely.

This section covers writing principles, vocabulary (terms you use, terms you avoid, how you refer to your own products), grammar and mechanics decisions - Oxford comma, sentence case or title case, UK or US English, date and number formats - and, most usefully, tone modulation: how the voice shifts between a celebratory announcement, an error message, a legal notice and a service outage.

Include worked examples. A rewritten paragraph teaches more than a page of adjectives.

### 8. Applications

Templates and worked examples for the things you actually produce: business cards, letterheads, email signatures, presentation decks, social templates per platform, ad formats, packaging, signage, vehicle livery, uniforms, exhibition stands.

This is what converts a brand book from a document people admire into a system people use. The best brand books ship with the working files attached.

### 9. Governance

The unglamorous part that determines whether any of it survives. Who owns the brand. Who approves exceptions. Where the assets live. How often the book is reviewed. What the process is when someone needs something the book doesn’t cover - because that will happen within the first month.

A brand book without a named owner degrades quietly. Within two years there are four versions of the logo in circulation and nobody remembers which is current.

## How long this takes, and who needs to be in the room

Two practical questions that determine whether the book gets built properly or gets built twice.

Timeline. A brand book for a mid-sized organisation typically takes eight to fourteen weeks end to end. Roughly: two to three weeks on strategy and stakeholder interviews, three to four on identity design and iteration, two to three on the extended system - colour, type, photography, iconography, voice - and two to three on applications, documentation and handover. Compressing this is possible; compressing the strategy phase is where it goes wrong, because everything downstream is then a matter of opinion.

People. The single biggest predictor of a brand book that survives is who was involved in making it.

- A decision-maker with actual authority. Not a committee. Design by committee produces the average of everyone’s preferences, which is beige by construction.
- Whoever runs sales. They will use this more than marketing does and they know what objections the brand has to answer.
- Whoever runs the product or the service. The brand promise has to be one the operation can keep.
- The people who will use it daily - the in-house designer, the social manager, the person who builds the decks. Their questions during development are the questions the book needs to answer.
- Someone from HR, if recruitment matters to you. Employer brand and customer brand share a system whether you plan it or not.

And one absent party worth naming: the CEO’s spouse, who traditionally reviews the logo at the weekend and has thoughts about the blue. If senior leadership will consult informally, get them into the process formally, early, where the strategy can inform the reaction.

## The honest test

Hand your brand book to a designer who has never worked with you. Ask them to produce three things you’ve never made - a recruitment poster, an app onboarding screen, a trade show banner.

If what comes back looks like your brand, you have a brand book. If they had to phone and ask questions, you have a logo sheet, and you’ve been paying for the gap ever since.

posts.title: SEO in the Age of AI Answers: What Changed, What Didn’t
posts.excerpt: AI Overviews, ChatGPT and Perplexity have rewired how people find things. Here’s what changed in SEO, what stayed the same and what to do about it.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity handles on-page and off-page SEO alongside the structural and entity work that gets brands cited in AI answers. Explore our digital services or ask us for a visibility audit across both search and generative platforms.
posts.body:
For about twenty years, SEO had a beautifully simple mental model. Someone types a question. Google returns ten blue links. You want to be one of them, ideally near the top. Everything - keywords, backlinks, technical hygiene - served that single objective.

That model has developed a significant crack.

AI Overviews now appear on roughly 48% of tracked queries, up about 58% year on year. ChatGPT reached around 900 million weekly active users as of early 2026. A meaningful share of searches now end with a synthesised answer rather than a click, and being ranked first matters considerably less if the answer above you already satisfied the question.

The temptation is to declare SEO dead, which is both dramatic and wrong. What’s actually happened is a split: the old game continues, and a second game has started next to it with overlapping but distinct rules.

## What genuinely changed

Visibility is now about citation, not just ranking. When an AI system answers a question, it typically cites two to seven sources. That’s the new front page - and it’s a much smaller front page than ten blue links.

Ranking and citation have come apart. This is the finding that should worry anyone still reporting on positions alone. Ahrefs found the overlap between top-10 organic results and AI Overview citations fell from 76% in July 2025 to 38% within eight months. Even more striking: 28.3% of ChatGPT’s most-cited pages have zero organic visibility in Google.

Read that again. More than a quarter of the pages an AI system leans on most heavily don’t rank at all in traditional search. Whatever earns citation, it isn’t purely the same thing that earns rankings.

Structure and completeness now outrank keyword placement. Traditional SEO rewarded keyword targeting and link acquisition. Generative systems reward semantic clarity, contextual completeness and extractability - content that can be understood, chunked and confidently quoted.

Zero-click became the default assumption. A growing share of informational queries resolve without a visit. Traffic can decline while brand visibility increases, which makes single-metric reporting actively misleading.

The measurement stack changed. SEO tracks rankings, impressions and clicks. GEO tracks citations, share of voice inside AI answers, and how your brand is described when it’s mentioned. Most organisations are still measuring only the first set and drawing conclusions about the second.

## What emphatically did not change

Before overcorrecting, note what still works exactly as it did.

Technical fundamentals. If a crawler can’t reach, render and parse your page, no system will cite it. Site architecture, crawlability, speed, mobile rendering, clean HTML - all unchanged, and arguably more important, since AI crawlers are less forgiving than Googlebot.

Genuine expertise. Content demonstrating real experience and authority performed well before and performs well now. AI systems are trained to prefer authoritative sources; thin content that scraped by on keyword targeting has simply lost its last hiding place.

Search intent. Understanding what someone actually wants when they type a query remains the whole discipline. Nothing about generative answers changes that.

Brand. People and machines both favour known entities. Building a brand people search for by name is still the most durable SEO strategy available, and it just got more valuable.

Original data. Proprietary research, original surveys and first-hand analysis were always the strongest link magnets. They’re now also the strongest citation magnets, because an AI answering a question needs a source for the number, and there’s only one of you.

## What to actually do

Structure content for extraction. Answer the question in the first 40 to 60 words, then elaborate. Use descriptive headings phrased as questions. Keep paragraphs tight. Put definitions, statistics and comparisons in clearly bounded, self-contained blocks. You’re writing for a system that will lift a chunk out of context - make every chunk survive the journey.

Implement structured data seriously. Schema markup for organisations, articles, FAQs, products, people and events gives machines unambiguous facts instead of inference. This is now table stakes.

Build entity clarity. AI systems reason about entities, not strings. Your organisation should be consistently described across your site, Wikipedia if you qualify, industry directories, LinkedIn and press coverage. Inconsistent descriptions produce a fuzzy entity, and fuzzy entities don’t get cited.

Publish original data. The single highest-leverage move available. One annual survey of your industry, published with methodology, will earn more citations than fifty listicles. It is also the one thing a competitor cannot copy.

Chase mentions, not just links. Unlinked brand mentions have been found to predict AI search visibility roughly three times better than backlinks. Digital PR that gets you described accurately on authoritative sites now works twice - once for traditional authority, once for generative visibility.

Measure both games. Add citation tracking to your reporting: which AI platforms mention you, for which queries, alongside whom, and in what terms. Then report traffic and citation separately, because a quarter where traffic dips and citations rise is not a bad quarter, and you’ll need the data to prove it.

Don’t abandon keywords. Traditional search is still enormous and still converts. GEO is additive, not a replacement. Anyone telling you to stop doing SEO is selling something.

## How these systems actually pick a source

It helps to understand the mechanics, because they explain why some of the advice above works and why a lot of conventional SEO advice doesn’t transfer.

When a generative system answers a question, it typically breaks the query into sub- questions, retrieves candidate passages for each, and assembles an answer from the passages it can most confidently support. The unit of retrieval is a passage, not a page. This is the single most important structural insight available, and it has three consequences.

Your page competes chunk by chunk. A 3,000-word guide isn’t one entry in the contest - it’s forty passages, each independently retrievable. A page can be cited for one specific paragraph while the rest is ignored entirely. Which means burying your best, most quotable, most specific sentence in paragraph 34 under a heading called “Some Considerations” is a genuine cost.

Ambiguous passages get skipped. A paragraph that begins “As mentioned above, this approach…” is unusable out of context, so it doesn’t get used. Passages that restate their subject - “Core Web Vitals are measured at the 75th percentile of real users” rather than “these are measured at the 75th percentile” - travel intact and get quoted.

Corroboration beats authority. Systems favour claims they can support from multiple independent sources. A figure that appears only on your site is harder to cite confidently than one that appears on yours and three others. This is the mechanical reason brand mentions matter so much: being described consistently in many places makes you a safer thing to say.

None of this requires new tooling. It requires writing paragraphs that make sense on their own - which, conveniently, is also better writing for humans.

## The uncomfortable strategic question

Here’s what most organisations haven’t sat down with yet: if a growing share of your audience gets their answer without visiting you, what is your website for?

Increasingly, it’s for two things. It’s the source of truth that AI systems read to describe you - which makes accuracy, structure and completeness commercially important in a way they never were. And it’s the destination for high-intent visitors who’ve already been pre- qualified by an AI answer and arrive further down the funnel than any visitor did five years ago.

That second group is smaller and considerably more valuable. Which suggests the sensible response isn’t to fight for volume that’s leaving anyway - it’s to make sure the machines describe you accurately, and to make sure the fewer, warmer people who do arrive find a page built for someone ready to act.

posts.title: On-Page vs. Off-Page in 2026: An Honest Audit Checklist
posts.excerpt: What still moves rankings on your own site, what has to be earned elsewhere and a practical audit checklist updated for search in 2026.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity runs on-page and off-page SEO as one programme, because separating them is how sites end up beautifully optimised and completely unknown. Explore our digital services or request an audit.
posts.body:
The on-page/off-page distinction has survived two decades of algorithm upheaval for one boring, excellent reason: it maps to control. On-page is what you can change this afternoon. Off-page is what you have to earn from other people, on their timeline, with their permission.

The split still holds. What’s changed dramatically is the weighting inside each half - and if your audit template is more than two years old, it’s optimising for a version of search that no longer exists.

Here’s an honest checklist for both, with the things that have quietly stopped mattering marked as such.

## On-page: what you control

### Content quality and depth

Still the foundation, still where most audits are too polite.

- Does the page fully satisfy the query? Not “does it mention the keyword” - does someone arriving with that question leave without needing another tab?
- Is there genuine first-hand expertise? Original analysis, real data, actual experience. Content assembled from the top five results is now competing against a machine that can assemble it faster and for free.
- Is it structured for extraction? Answer-first paragraphs, question-phrased headings, self-contained blocks for definitions and statistics. This matters for both featured snippets and AI citation.
- Is it current? Date-stamped, reviewed, with outdated figures actually replaced rather than quietly left in.
- Is there a reason to read yours specifically? If not, no amount of technical work will save it.

### Technical foundation

- Crawlability - robots.txt sane, no accidental noindex, XML sitemap accurate and submitted
- Indexation - check what’s actually indexed versus what you think is; thin and duplicate pages should be pruned, not tolerated
- Site architecture - every important page reachable within three clicks of the homepage
- Internal linking - descriptive anchor text, links from high-authority pages to pages that need help, no orphans
- Canonicals - self-referencing where appropriate, correct on paginated and parameterised URLs
- Core Web Vitals - LCP under 2.5s, INP under 200ms, CLS under 0.1, measured at the 75th percentile of real users
- Mobile rendering - not “responsive,” genuinely tested on real devices
- HTTPS, no mixed content, clean redirect chains
- AI crawler access - verify you aren’t inadvertently blocking the crawlers used by generative platforms

### Structured data

Now materially more important than it was.

- Organisation schema, consistent with every other description of you online
- Article, FAQ, Product, Event, Person as applicable
- Breadcrumb markup
- Validated - invalid schema is worse than none

### Meta and headings

- Title tags - unique, descriptive, primary term near the front, under about 60 characters
- Meta descriptions - they don’t influence ranking, they influence clicks. Write them like ad copy.
- One H1 per page, describing the actual content
- Heading hierarchy that reflects structure rather than font size preferences
- Image alt text that describes the image, for accessibility first and search second

### Quietly stopped mattering

Keyword density. Exact-match keywords in every heading. Meta keywords tag - still, somehow, present in audits in 2026. Rigid word-count targets. Manually forcing LSI keywords in.

## Off-page: what you earn

This is where the weighting shift has been most dramatic.

Backlinks now account for roughly 45% of off-page ranking weight, down from around 80% in 2012. Brand mentions and entity signals make up the remaining 55%. The old off-page playbook is optimising for less than half the picture.

### Brand mentions and entity signals

- Unlinked mentions on authoritative sites - now a valid signal in their own right, and they’ve been found to predict AI search visibility roughly three times better than backlinks
- Entity consistency - is your organisation described the same way across your site, LinkedIn, directories, press and Wikipedia? Inconsistency produces a blurry entity, and blurry entities get overlooked
- Co-citation - do you appear alongside the right companies in industry roundups and comparisons?
- Branded search volume - the health metric almost nobody tracks. Growth here indicates everything else is working

### Links, judged properly

- Relevance over authority - a link from a mid-tier site in your sector beats a high-DA link from an unrelated one
- Editorial placement - earned within real content, not a footer or a sponsored block
- Anchor diversity - natural profiles are mostly branded and generic anchors, not exact-match
- Referring domain growth - steady growth over spikes; spikes are a pattern, and patterns get inspected
- Toxic link review - done occasionally, not obsessively; most low-quality links are simply ignored

### Digital PR and original research

Digital PR has replaced traditional link building as the highest-ROI off-page activity, because it produces links and brand signals simultaneously. Campaigns combining brand mention monitoring, co-citation analysis and entity optimisation have been reported to lift keyword group rankings by around 18% over link-only approaches.

The most reliable engine remains original research. One well-executed industry survey, published with methodology, generates coverage, links, mentions and citations for years. It is also the one asset a competitor genuinely cannot replicate.

### The rest of the footprint

- YouTube presence - increasingly surfaced in both traditional and AI search
- Reviews and ratings on the platforms your buyers actually check
- Community participation - Reddit, Quora, industry forums, professional communities, where being genuinely helpful builds entity presence
- Google Business Profile - complete and current, if you have any local dimension

### Quietly stopped mattering

Directory submissions at volume. Article spinning. Comment links. Private blog networks - which now carry meaningful risk. Chasing Domain Authority as a target rather than a diagnostic.

## How to actually run the audit

Two passes, in order.

Pass one: technical and on-page. Crawl the site, fix what’s broken, prune what’s thin, structure what’s salvageable. This is fast, entirely within your control, and often produces the quickest gains - particularly on sites that have never been pruned.

Pass two: authority and entity. Map your current mention and link footprint, identify where competitors appear and you don’t, and build a digital PR plan around one substantial original asset per quarter.

The sequencing matters. Building authority to a site with structural problems is pouring water into a leaking bucket, and you’ll spend months wondering why the numbers won’t move.

## Cadence: how often to actually do this

A full audit is a project. Treating it as an annual event is why sites drift. A sensible rhythm:

Weekly (15 minutes). Check Search Console for new coverage errors, manual actions and sudden impression drops. Most disasters announce themselves here first, quietly, several weeks before anyone notices the traffic.

Monthly (half a day). Review Core Web Vitals field data, top-page performance, new referring domains and lost ones, and any new brand mentions. Update or prune the three worst-performing pages rather than writing three new ones - refreshing existing content is consistently better value than adding to the pile.

Quarterly (two to three days). Run the full technical crawl. Re-check indexation against intent. Review internal linking on newly published clusters. Ship one substantial original asset - research, a tool, a benchmark - as the quarter’s off-page engine.

Annually (a week). Revisit strategy properly: which pages earn revenue, which topics you actually deserve to own, which competitors have moved, and what should be deleted. Deletion is the most underrated SEO activity in existence. A site of 200 excellent pages consistently outperforms one with 200 excellent pages and 1,400 mediocre ones.

One standing rule: before publishing anything new, check whether an existing page should have been updated instead. Most sites have a cannibalisation problem they built themselves, one well-intentioned blog post at a time.

posts.title: Core Web Vitals for Marketers: The Three Numbers That Matter
posts.excerpt: LCP, INP and CLS explained without engineering jargon: what each measures, what good looks like and what to ask your developers.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity builds sites where performance is a design decision rather than a post-launch panic. Explore our web and app development or ask us to look at your field data - we’ll tell you which three pages to fix first.
posts.body:
Your developer says the site is “performing well.” Your agency’s report shows a big green circle. Meanwhile your bounce rate on mobile is 68% and the paid traffic you’re buying seems to evaporate somewhere between the click and the page.

Somewhere in this gap sit three numbers. They have unfriendly acronyms, they’re measured in units nobody uses in conversation, and they quietly govern both how your site ranks and whether visitors stay long enough to convert.

You don’t need to know how to fix them. You do need to know what they are, what “good” looks like, and how to tell whether the green circle is telling you the truth. That’s a fifteen- minute investment with an unusually good return.

## The one thing to understand first

Core Web Vitals are measured on real visitors, not in a lab.

Google evaluates them at the 75th percentile of your actual traffic. Which means: three out of four visitors must have a good experience for the URL to pass. Not your average visitor. Not your developer on office fibre with a warm cache and a new laptop.

This single fact explains most of the confusion in performance reporting. A lab test - the kind that produces the satisfying green score - simulates one visit under controlled conditions. Field data records what actually happened to real people on a patchy 4G connection in a lift.

If your lab score is excellent and your field data is failing, the field data is right. It’s not a measurement error. It’s your audience.

## LCP - Largest Contentful Paint

What it measures: how long until the main content appears. Usually the hero image, the headline, or the big block that makes the page feel arrived.

Good: under 2.5 seconds. Needs work: 2.5 to 4 seconds. Poor: over 4 seconds.

Why it matters commercially: LCP is roughly “how long the page felt blank.” It maps almost directly to bounce rate on paid traffic, because someone who clicked an ad and got a white screen has no loyalty to spend on waiting.

Usual culprits: an enormous unoptimised hero image, slow server response, render- blocking scripts, web fonts that delay text, and - perennially - a tag manager container carrying eleven marketing scripts, several of which belong to campaigns that ended in 2023.

What to ask: “What’s our LCP element on the main landing pages, and what’s delaying it?” A good developer will name the element and the blocker in one sentence.

## INP - Interaction to Next Paint

What it measures: how quickly the page visibly responds when someone interacts - taps a button, opens a menu, types in a field. It replaced First Input Delay in 2024 and is a considerably harsher, more honest metric, because it measures all interactions across the visit rather than just the first one.

Good: under 200 milliseconds. Needs work: 200 to 500ms. Poor: over 500ms.

Why it matters commercially: INP is the “is this thing broken?” metric. A tap that doesn’t respond within about 200ms feels unresponsive, and the universal human response is to tap again - which frequently triggers a duplicate submission, then confusion, then abandonment.

Worth knowing: INP is the most commonly failed Core Web Vital in 2026, with around 43% of sites still missing the 200ms threshold. If you’re going to fail one, statistically this is it.

Usual culprits: heavy JavaScript blocking the main thread, oversized third-party scripts, chat widgets, A/B testing tools, and analytics stacks that have accumulated like sediment over several agency relationships.

What to ask: “Which interactions have the worst INP, and what’s blocking the main thread when they happen?”

## CLS - Cumulative Layout Shift

What it measures: how much the page jumps around while loading. It’s a unitless score, not a time.

Good: under 0.1. Needs work: 0.1 to 0.25. Poor: over 0.25.

Why it matters commercially: CLS is the metric behind the universally infuriating experience of reaching for a link and having an ad load above it, so you tap something else entirely. It damages trust immediately and correlates with form abandonment - and it’s the one your customers will actually complain about, because it’s the only one they can see happening.

Usual culprits: images without width and height attributes, ads and embeds injected without reserved space, web fonts causing text to reflow, cookie banners appearing late, and dynamically inserted content pushing everything down.

Good news: CLS is usually the cheapest of the three to fix. Reserving space for known elements is straightforward engineering, and the improvement is often dramatic and immediate.

What to ask: “Which elements are shifting, and can we reserve space for them?”

## Reading the report without being misled

Field data beats lab data. Always. In PageSpeed Insights, the top section is real-user data from the Chrome User Experience Report. The bottom section is a simulated Lighthouse test. Marketers habitually quote the Lighthouse score because it’s a single tidy number. It’s the less important one.

Check by page type, not sitewide. Your homepage might pass while your highest-spend landing page fails. Since Core Web Vitals are assessed at URL level, sitewide averages can hide exactly the pages you’re paying to send traffic to.

Separate mobile and desktop. They’re measured separately and they usually differ substantially. Mobile is where the problems live and where most of your traffic is.

Set alerts below the thresholds. A sensible early-warning practice is to alert at roughly 80% of Google’s limits - INP above 160ms, LCP above 2.0s, CLS above 0.08 - so you catch drift before it becomes a failure.

## Fixing them in the right order

You’re not going to do the engineering, but you are going to prioritise it - and prioritisation is where most performance projects waste their budget, because teams start with whatever is most technically interesting rather than whatever is most commercially expensive.

A workable order:

1. Fix CLS first. It’s usually the cheapest, the fastest and the most visible to users. Reserving space for images, ads and banners is well-understood work with an immediate, obvious result. Good for morale, good for the visitor, cheap.

2. Audit your third-party scripts. This one fix frequently improves both LCP and INP simultaneously, and it’s a marketing decision rather than an engineering one. Open your tag manager, list every script, and identify who owns each and what it’s for. On most sites, a third of them are orphans from campaigns, vendors or agencies that are no longer involved.
