Removing them costs nothing and requires no code.

3. Attack LCP on your highest-spend pages. Not sitewide - start where the money lands. Compress and correctly size the hero image, serve modern formats, preload the LCP element, and check server response time. Fixing three landing pages is a fortnight’s work; fixing the whole site is a quarter’s.

4. Then INP. This is the genuinely hard one, because it usually means reducing or deferring JavaScript, which touches how the site is built. It’s a roadmap item, not a sprint task. Budget for it honestly rather than promising it by Friday.

One warning: performance regresses. It always regresses. A site fixed in March fails again by September because six new scripts, a chat widget and a video embed have arrived in the meantime. Put field data on a monthly dashboard someone actually looks at, or you’ll be commissioning this project again next year.

## What this is actually worth

Two honest caveats.

First, Core Web Vitals are a genuine but modest ranking factor. They’re a tiebreaker between comparably relevant pages, not a substitute for relevance. Nobody has ever out- ranked better content by having a faster page.

Second, and more importantly: the conversion impact is generally larger than the ranking impact. A page that loads fast, responds immediately and doesn’t move around converts better than one that doesn’t, regardless of what Google thinks. That’s the business case, and it doesn’t depend on any algorithm continuing to care.

Which reframes the whole conversation. Core Web Vitals aren’t an SEO chore to be tolerated. They’re a proxy for whether your site is pleasant to use - and that has never needed a search engine’s endorsement to matter.

posts.title: Why Your Ads Work but Your Landing Page Doesn’t
posts.excerpt: Great click-through rate, terrible conversion rate? Here’s how message match, offer relevance and page design leak your advertising budget.
posts.author: Latch Infinity
posts.cta: Latch Infinity builds ads and the pages they land on as a single system, because the handoff between them is where most media budgets quietly disappear. Explore our advertising services or send us a campaign to diagnose.
posts.body:
The campaign report is a study in contrasts.

Click-through rate: excellent. Cost per click: comfortably under target. The creative is being praised in the review meeting. And then, at the bottom of the page, conversions - a number so small that someone has to check the tracking is even working.

The instinctive response is to blame the ad. Wrong audience, wrong creative, wrong platform. But an ad with a strong CTR has already proven it can attract the right person and interest them. That job is finished, and it was done well.

The leak is downstream. And it’s almost always one of three things.

## First, know what “bad” actually is

Before diagnosing, calibrate - because plenty of “underperforming” pages are actually fine, and plenty of “acceptable” ones are quietly terrible.

Median landing page conversion rates across industries in 2026 sit somewhere around 4% to 4.3%, with meaningful variation by sector: ecommerce around 3.1%, SaaS free trials near 7.2%, home services lead-gen as high as 8.5%. Notably, dedicated landing pages convert at roughly double the rate of general website pages - around 4% versus 2.35%.

That last comparison is the first diagnostic. If your ads point at your homepage or a general product page, you’re starting at half the achievable rate before anything else goes wrong.

## Leak one: message match

This is the biggest and the most common. Around 60% of audited pages have weak or no message match, and when visitors click an ad promising one thing and arrive at a page delivering something adjacent, bounce rates spike above 70%.

Message match means the ad and the page agree - on headline, offer, imagery, tone and specificity. The visitor should land and feel their click was confirmed, not questioned.

The classic failures:

The ad is specific, the page is general. Ad: “Compliance-ready e-learning for UGC- approved programmes.” Page: “Welcome to our digital solutions.” The visitor now has to work out whether they’re in the right place - and they won’t; they’ll go back.

The offer changes. Ad promises a free audit. Page offers a demo booking. Small difference to you, complete bait-and-switch to them.

The visual language breaks. The ad had a distinctive image. The page has a stock photo of a handshake. Recognition is lost in the half-second where it mattered most.

The specificity drops. Ad names a number, a timeframe or an outcome. The page speaks only in benefits. The concrete promise that earned the click has evaporated.

The fix is unglamorous and effective: put the ad and the page side by side on one screen. Does the page headline contain the ad’s promise, close to word for word? Is the offer identical? Would a stranger, shown both, believe they belong together? If any answer is no, you’ve found your leak - and it’s usually worth more than any amount of creative testing.

## Leak two: the offer doesn’t match the intent

Conversion rate is broadly a function of three things: traffic quality, message match, and offer relevance. The third is where campaigns fail more subtly.

Someone who clicked an ad about a problem they’re researching is not ready for “Book a 45-minute consultation.” That’s a large ask for a cold visitor - you’re requesting their calendar, their phone number and their afternoon before they know whether you’re any good.

Match the ask to the temperature. Cold traffic from awareness content converts on low- commitment offers: a guide, a checklist, a benchmark report, a calculator. Warm traffic from retargeting or high-intent search converts on demos, quotes and trials. Running one offer across all traffic guarantees you’re over-asking half your audience and under-asking the other half.

A practical test: if your page has one CTA and it’s your highest-commitment action, add a secondary, lower-commitment option. The lift is often immediate - and the low- commitment converts feed a nurture sequence that produces the high-commitment ones later.

## Leak three: the page itself

Once message and offer are right, ordinary page problems become the constraint.

Above the fold isn’t doing its job. The visitor should know, without scrolling: what this is, who it’s for, what they get, and what to do next. Most pages spend that space on a brand statement.

The form is too long. Every field costs conversions. Ask for what you need to make the next contact useful and nothing else. “Company size” can wait until you’re speaking.

No proof. Claims without evidence are decoration. Named clients, specific outcomes, real testimonials with real names, certifications, numbers. Anonymous praise from “CEO, Leading Firm” reads as fabricated, because it usually is.

Too many exits. A landing page with full site navigation is offering the visitor twelve ways to leave. Strip it. This is the single easiest fix in the entire list.

Slow or unstable. If the page takes four seconds to render its main content, a meaningful share of your paid traffic never sees it. If the layout jumps as they reach for the button, they tap the wrong thing. You paid for those clicks.

Mobile designed second. Most paid social traffic is on a phone. If the desktop version was designed first and the mobile version derived from it, the form is probably below three scrolls of hero image.

## Fixing it in order

Diagnose, don’t guess. Run this sequence:

1. Check the bounce rate. Above 70% on paid traffic points to message match, almost always.

2. Compare ad and page side by side. Fix the headline first - it’s the highest-leverage element on the page.

3. Audit the ask against traffic temperature. Add a lower-commitment offer if there isn’t one.

4. Cut the form to essential fields only. 5. Remove navigation and every non-converting link. 6. Check field performance data on mobile specifically. 7. Then, and only then, start A/B testing.

That order matters. Testing button colours on a page with broken message match is measuring the wrong thing very precisely - and it’s how teams spend six weeks improving a page by 2% when a headline rewrite was worth 40%.

Before you fix anything: is the tracking lying to you?

A genuinely uncomfortable share of “landing page problems” turn out to be measurement problems. Worth ruling out before you rebuild anything.

Consent banners eating conversions. If your consent management platform blocks analytics until the visitor accepts, and a meaningful share never accept, you are simply not seeing those conversions. The page may be converting fine. Your dashboard is just looking away.

Attribution windows that don’t match the sales cycle. A seven-day click window on a product with a six-week consideration cycle will systematically under-credit the campaign. The conversions are happening. They’re being filed under “direct” three weeks later.

Thank-you pages that don’t fire. The classic. A form redirects, the tag doesn’t load, and an entire quarter of leads exists in the CRM but not the ad platform. Test it yourself. Actually submit the form. You’d be surprised how many people never have.

Cross-device journeys. Someone sees the ad on a phone at 11pm and converts on a laptop on Tuesday. Without logged-in or server-side measurement, that’s two people as far as your platform is concerned, one of whom bounced.

Comparing the wrong denominators. Ad platform conversion rate, analytics conversion rate and CRM-qualified lead rate are three different numbers measuring three different things. Teams routinely compare one quarter’s figure from one system with the next quarter’s from another and draw firm conclusions.

Spend an hour verifying the numbers before you spend a month fixing a page. Sometimes the page is fine and the dashboard needs the intervention.

## The uncomfortable conclusion

If your ads are working and your page isn’t, the campaign isn’t underperforming. It’s subsidising a page problem - paying full price for qualified attention and then discarding most of it at the door.

Which is oddly good news. Attracting the right person is the hard, expensive part, and you’ve already solved it. What’s left is making sure the page keeps the promise the ad made.
